name: Zbigniew Dacewicz
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 34611/97) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged that after having been arrested he had not been brought before a “judge” or “officer authorised by law to exercise judicial power”. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. In a decision of 21 June 2001 the Court declared the application admissible. This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. The case is now before the European Court of Human rights (ECHR) In 1996 the applicant complained that he had not been brought before a judge but before the Biała Podlaska District Prosecutor. The Supreme Court dismissed the complaint as an appeal against the detention order of 4 January 1996. The court considered that the applicant should be detained because there was a reasonable risk that he might obstruct the proper conduct of the proceedings. Under the amendments to Polish criminal legislation, which were to enter into force on 4 August 1996, only the courts of law could impose detention on remand. On 23 June 1996 the court gave judgment and convicted the applicant of dealing with stolen goods. The applicant was found guilty and sentenced to three years in prison.

The case originated in an application (no. 34611/97) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that after having been arrested he had not been brought before a “judge” or “officer authorised by law to exercise judicial power”. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 of the Rule of Court. By a decision of 21 June 2001 the Court declared the application admissible. This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. The applicant complained to the Supreme Court that he had not been brought before a judge but before the Biała Podlaska District Prosecutor. The court considered that the applicant should be detained because there was a reasonable risk that he might obstruct the proper conduct of the proceedings. Under the amendments to Polish criminal legislation, which were to enter into force on 4 August 1996, only the courts of law could impose detention on remand. The applicant was found guilty of dealing with stolen goods on 23 June 1996 and sentenced to two years in prison. The case was dismissed on 26 June 1996 after the judge ruled that the detention had been unlawful under the Code of Criminal Procedure.

Case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged, in particular, that after having been arrested he had not been brought before a “judge” or “officer authorised by law to exercise judicial power” The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998. By a decision of 21 June 2001 the Court declared the application admissible. This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section of the Court. The case was heard by the European Court of Justice (ECJ) between 19 and 25 June 2002. The applicant complained to the Supreme Court that he had not been brought before a judge but before the Biała Podlaska District Prosecutor. The court deemed the complaint to be an appeal against the detention order of 4 January 1996. Under the amendments to Polish criminal legislation, which were to enter into force on 4 August 1996, only the courts of law could impose detention on remand. On 23 June 1996 the court gave judgment and convicted the applicant of dealing with stolen goods. The Supreme Court ruled that the detention of the applicant was unlawful because the order was made by the prosecutor, who did not have the attributes of a ‘judge’ required by law.

name: Barbara Warsicka
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 2065/03) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant, the owner of real property which she had been renting, filed a civil action for damages against the tenant. Her appeal was dismissed by a judgment of the Poznań Court of Appeal. On 22 October 2001 her cassation appeal was rejected by a decision of that panel. The Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. The court noted the case-law of the Supreme Court on the interpretation of Article 393 3 § 1 (3) of the Code. It referred to the applicant’s objection in one sentence only: “The fact that the judge, who took part in the judgment against which the cassation appeal was subsequently lodged, participated in a decision by which this appeal was found inadmissible is of no significance”. The same judge had sat on a panel giving a second-instance judgment on the merits and subsequently on an appeal panel rejecting that judgment. The court noted that this requirement was closely linked to the examination of the grounds on which the Court could refuse to entertain an appeal.

name: Arthur Collins Redfearn
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 47335/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained, among other things, that he had been dismissed on account of his political views and membership of a political party. The application was examined at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 1). The Government was represented by their Agent, Mr D. Walton of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The case was heard by the Fourth Section of the Court on 7 January 2009 and the decision was made to allow the application to be heard. The BNP councillor was dismissed by Serco in 2004 after being elected as a local councillor for the BNP. The union UNISON asked Serco to take immediate action to ensure its members were not subjected to racial hatred. The applicant claimed that he had been unlawfully discriminated against as his dismissal constituted less favourable treatment on racial grounds. Serco cited potential health and safety risks as the applicant’s continued employment would give rise to considerable anxiety among passengers and their carers. It also expressed concern that the applicant's continued employment could jeopardise its reputation and possibly lead to the loss of its contract with Bradford City Council. The Employment Tribunal gave judgment on 2 February 2005. The Employment Tribunal dismissed the claim of direct discrimination as it was satisfied that if any discrimination existed against the claimant it was not on racial grounds but rather on health and safety grounds. Mr Redfearn lodged an appeal with the Employment Appeal Tribunal. On 27 July 2005 his appeal was upheld on the ground that the Tribunal had erred in its construction of the phrase ‘on racial grounds’ by failing to interpret its meaning broadly. The Court of Appeal allowed Serco’s appeal and restored the order of the Employment Tribunal. Mummery LJ found the applicant's submission that he was subjected to direct race discrimination to be wrong in principle and inconsistent with the purposes of the legislation. The BNP cannot make a non-racial criterion (party membership) a racial one by the terms of its constitution limiting membership to white people. Properly analysed Mr Redfearn’s complaint is of discrimination on political grounds, which falls outside the anti-discrimination laws. The employment tribunal appears to have attempted itself a version of a ‘provision, criterion or practice’ in paragraph 5.6 of its decision (see paragraph 28 above) However, it is formulated too narrowly (membership of the BNP) to be meaningful. A more general and meaningful provision along similar lines would be one applying to membership of a political organisation like BNP, which existed to promote views hostile to members of a different colour. The applicant was refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords. 1976 Act are incompatible with the Convention rights. As for justification under the 1976 Act I have already explained that it does not arise, as no case of indirect discrimination has been made out.” The application was rejected by the Court of Appeal on Tuesday. The appeal was rejected on Wednesday and the decision cannot be appealed to the Lords. The case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights on Wednesday. The judge said that the case was not a case of direct discrimination, but of ‘indirect discrimination’. The hearing was adjourned until later this month.

The case originated in an application (no. 47335/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained, among other things, that he had been dismissed on account of his political views and membership of a political party. The application was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 1) The case was heard on 7 January 2009. The decision to admit the application was made at the request of the applicant, Mr Arthur Collins Redfearn, and the Government of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. In 2004 the applicant was elected as a local councillor for the BNP. Serco summarily dismissed him on 30 June 2004. He lodged a statutory claim of race discrimination in the Employment Tribunal pursuant to the Race Relations Act 1976 (“the 1976 Act”) The Employment Tribunal gave judgment on 2 February 2005. The applicant claimed that he had been unlawfully discriminated against as his dismissal constituted less favourable treatment on racial grounds. The racial grounds relied on were those of the passengers and employees of Serco who were of Asian origin. He further argued that since the BJP was a “whites-only” party, his dismissal also constituted indirect racial discrimination. Employment Tribunal dismissed the claim of direct discrimination as it was satisfied that if any discrimination existed against the claimant it was not on racial grounds but rather on health and safety grounds. Tribunal also dismissed claim of indirect discrimination on the ground that the applicant’s dismissal was a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim. Mr Redfearn lodged an appeal with the Employment Appeal Tribunal. On 27 July 2005 his appeal was upheld on the grounds that the Tribunal had erred in its construction of the phrase ‘on racial grounds’ by failing to interpret its meaning broadly and had not indicated how it had come to the conclusion that it had. Serco was not adopting a policy which discriminated on the basis of a dividing line of colour or race. The BNP cannot make a non-racial criterion (party membership) a racial one by the terms of its constitution limiting membership to white people. Properly analysed Mr Redfearn’s complaint is of discrimination on political grounds, which falls outside the anti-discrimination laws. The employment tribunal appears to have attempted itself a version of a ‘provision, criterion or practice’ in paragraph 5.6 of its decision. However, it is formulated too narrowly (membership of the BNP) to be meaningful. A more general and meaningful provision along similar lines would be one applying to membership of a political organisation. The applicant was refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords. 1976 Act are incompatible with the Convention rights. As for justification under the 1976 Act I have already explained that it does not arise, as no case of indirect discrimination has been made out.” The application was referred to the European Court of Human Rights in Brussels. The European Court of Human Rights found that the application was a breach of the European Convention on Human Rights. The application had been referred to by the European Commission in Brussels in Brussels as a violation of the Convention on human rights. The case was referred by the European Court of Human Rights in Brussels to the Supreme Court of Justice in London. The appeal was denied.

It noted Serco's concerns that the applicant’s continued employment might lead to difficulties with other employees; damage its relationship with the unions; lead to attacks on Serco”s minibuses which would jeopardise the health and safety of passengers and their carers. Employment Tribunal dismissed the claim of direct discrimination against the claimant. Serco would apply the same approach to a member of a similar political party, which confined its membership to black people. The dividing line of colour or race was not made by Serco, but by the BNP. The BNP cannot make a non-racial criterion (party membership) a racial one by the terms of its constitution limiting membership to white people. Mr Redfearn’s complaint is of discrimination on political grounds, which falls outside the anti-discrimination laws. The employment tribunal appears to have attempted itself a version of a ‘provision, criterion or practice’ in paragraph 5.6 of its decision (see paragraph 28 above). However, it is formulated too narrowly (membership of the BNP) to be meaningful. A more general and meaningful provision along similar lines would be one applying to membership of a political organisation, which existed to promote views hostile to members of a different colour. The applicant was refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords. 1976 Act are incompatible with the Convention rights. As for justification under the 1976 Act I have already explained that it does not arise, as no case of indirect discrimination has been made out.” The judge ruled that the application was not in breach of the Convention. The case was adjourned until after the election on June 6. The judge said he would return to the court on July 3 to consider the application again. The application was denied and the case was remanded in custody until the next hearing on July 16. The appeal was dismissed on July 9 and a new hearing will be held on July 18.

name: Makbule Özalp
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32457/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged, inter alia, that Cavit Özalp had been killed by the security forces while he was under custody and that there had been no effective investigation into the circumstances of his death. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 31 August 2000, the Court declared the application partly admissible. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1) and this case was assigned to the newly composed First Section. Cavit Özalp was killed in 1995 while he was under custody. The applicants' representatives filed a petition with the public prosecutor attached to the Diyarbakır State Security Court. They requested a copy of the arrest and autopsy reports as well as the publicProsecutor's decision of non-prosecution into Cavit's death. The petition was denied by the public Prosecutor. The application was returned to the court on 6 March 1996 and the case against the applicants was dismissed. The family moved from the Serçeler village in Bismil District in province of Diyartsar in the spring of 1994. In August 1995 one of the applicants, Mr Hacı ÖzAlp, went back to the fields that belonged to his family. He was stopped by soldiers and questioned about his father. Cavit Özalp was taken into custody by the gendarmes on suspicion of membership of the PKK, proscribed as a terrorist organisation. He was suspected of aiding and abetting the PKK terrorists. Cavit guided the soldiers to the shelter near the Şedat road in the Kamberli village. While protecting themselves in a secure distance, the soldiers asked him to open the cover of the shelter, which tore Cavit's body into pieces. The explosives had been placed in the entrance to the Shelter by other members of the. PKK and the soldiers found weapons, medical equipment and clothes in the shelter. According to the medical report, there were no signs of ill-treatment on his body. Cavit Özalp was killed in an explosion on 26 August 1995 in Diyarbakır. His legs were severed as a result of the explosion. No other signs of injury were observed on the dismembered body. An incident report was drafted by the gendarmes and was signed by three non-commissioned officers and the village mayor Mr Kütbettin Altunç. No prosecution should be brought against Cavit on account of his membership of the PKK on the ground that he had died on26 August 1995. An on-site examination was conducted by the Bismil public prosecutor and a doctor. Cavit Özalp was killed in an explosion when he tried to open a shelter. The explosives had been previously placed there by the terrorists. The report concluded that the security forces had performed their duty with diligence. The Bismil District Administrative Council issued a decision stating that no prosecution should be brought against the members of the security force. On 2 April 1996 the Diyarbakır Regional Administrative Court upheld the decision of the Bisml District Administrative council. The case had been automatically referred to the court by law. The court ruled that the case should be adjourned until a later date and that no action should be taken against any of the accused soldiers. The application was filed against Cavit Özalp in 1996. The application was rejected by the Diyarbakır State Security Court Public Prosecutor's office on 5 February 1996. A non-prosecution decision of the Bismil District Administrative Council was upheld on 2 April 1996, upholding the decision of that council. An application was also made against the applicants' representatives, Mr İlhan Yücel, Mr Yılmaz Öztiryaki and Mr Ömer Karabaş, dated 15 January 1996. It was rejected on 6 February 1996 by the public prosecutor's office. The applications were filed by Hacı and Makbule ÖzAlp.

The application was filed on behalf of the applicants' son, Hacı, who had been questioned about his father by the Turkish security forces in August 1995. It was filed to obtain a copy of the arrest and autopsy reports as well as the publicProsecutor's decision ofNon-Prosecution. Cavit Özalp was taken into custody by the gendarmes on suspicion of membership of the PKK, proscribed as a terrorist organisation. He was suspected of aiding and abetting the PKK terrorists. Cavit guided the soldiers to the shelter near the Şedat road in the Kamberli village. While protecting themselves in a secure distance, the soldiers asked him to open the cover of the shelter. As he opened the cover, the soldier witnessed a big explosion, which tore Cavit's body into pieces. The explosives had been placed in the entrance to the shelters by other members of the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) Cavit Özalp was killed by an explosion on 26 August 1995. The public prosecutor at the Diyarbakır State Security Court decided that no prosecution should be brought against Cavit on account of his membership of the PKK. The Bismil District Administrative Council appointed a major as a rapporteur to conduct further investigations into the killing. On 15 January 1996 the major took statements from the non-commissioned officers, Mr İlhan Yücel, Mr Yılmaz Öztiryaki and Mr Ömer Karabaş, who had been on site during the incident. The officers stated that Cavit had been taken into custody on suspicion of membership ofThe PKK and had confessed that he had been aiding and abetting the terrorists, providing them with food, clothes, weapons and medical equipment. Cavit Özalp died in an explosion after being asked to open the cover of the shelter. The explosives had been previously placed there by the terrorists. The report concluded that the security forces had performed their duty with diligence. The Bismil District Administrative Council issued a decision stating that no prosecution should be brought against the members of the security force. The Diyarbakır Regional Administrative Court upheld the decision of the Bismill district administrative council. The case was automatically referred to by law, and the decision was upheld by the court on 2 April 1996. The court ruled that the accused soldiers had not been responsible for the explosion. Cavit Özalp was convicted in relation to the murder of three Turkish police officers in 1996. He was sentenced to 15 years in prison. Cavit's trial was held in the Diyarbakır State Security Court Public Prosecutor's office. The trial took place between November 1995 and April 1996. The case was adjourned until May 1996, with the verdict delivered on April 2, 1996. His trial was the first to be held in Turkey's capital city, Istanbul, which was the scene of the alleged crime of murder of the three police officers, Mr İlhan Yücel, Mr Yılmaz Öztiryaki and Mr Ömer Karabaş. The verdict was delivered by the prosecutor's office on February 5, 1996, and upheld by the regional administrative court on March 2, 1997.

On 27 March 2003 an ambulance was called for the applicant since he had complained about pain in his abdomen. On that occasion, the applicant did not mention any injuries related to his allegedly ill- treatment and had received pain killers. The Bakırköy Assize Court found the applicant guilty of trafficking drugs and sentenced him to six years and three months’ imprisonment. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. On 21 April 2010 the applicant was granted conditional release. The court took into account the statements of the police officers, the testimony of M.T. and the evidence resulting from the police operation. the court rejected the request of the applicant’s lawyer to determine to whom those numbers belonged, noting that it would have no effect on the judgment. The applicant’s lawyer argued that police evidence was unlawful in that the officers had conducted the operation without any judicial supervision and that their acts amounted to inciting the commission of an offence. The judge agreed. The applicant was sentenced to six years and three months in prison for trafficking drugs. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. On 21 April 2010 the applicant was granted conditional release. The court took into account the statements of the police officers, the testimony of M.T. and the evidence resulting from the police operation against the applicant. The judge ruled that the evidence relied on by the public prosecutor had been obtained unlawfully. The trial took place in the city of Bakırköy, in the east of the country. The applicant is originally from the town of Ljubljana, the capital of Slovenia.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 26808/08) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. On 9 February 2010 the application was declared partly inadmissible. The Government objected to the examination of the application by a Committee. Taking into account the issues raised in the application, the Court finds it appropriate to allocate the case to a Chamber. The case was returned to the first-instance court on 16 September 2003. The applicant was born in 1962 and lives in Tokat. He was convicted of membership of an illegal organisation and involvement in a bank robbery in 2002 and sentenced to life imprisonment. The Istanbul Assize Court reviewed the necessity of the applicant’s continued pre-trial detention every thirty days on the basis of the case file. At those hearings the applicant made his pleadings orally before the trial court and requested to be released pending trial. At a hearing on 6 March 2008, the applicant claimed that his continued detention was unlawful. On 4 April 2008 the court dismissed the objection lodged by the applicant based on the public prosecutor's written opinion, which had not been communicated to the applicant. On 3 November 2009, having regard to the period he had spent in detention, the Istanbul Assizing Court released the applicant on the condition that he did not leave the country.

name: Falter Zeitschriften GmbH
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Falter Zeitschriften GmbH. The applicant company alleged that a court judgment under the Media Act ordering it to pay damages had infringed its right to freedom of expression. The application was communicated to the Government on 29 January 2009. It was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The judge ruled that the application was not admissible and that the case against the Austrian Government was dismissed. The case takes on a political dimension because it exposes conditions in the Traiskirchen centre. One year later only the victim is still before the courts. The chronicling of a judicial scandal. Elaine B. (name changed, ed.) had been ill-treated by police officers in Cameroon. She was kicked by them in the abdomen and placed with 18 other women in ‘stinking, damp cells’ for having demonstrated on behalf of her son, abducted by the authorities. She survived her escape on a container ship, during which she ‘nearly went mad’ and ‘no longer knew whether it was night or day outside’ With a thousand asylum seekers, Traiskirchen is hopelessly over­crowded. Another hundred arrive every day. The Interior Ministry is coming under political pressure and discredits Caritas. Security officers at the centre later state in court that female asylum seekers could be paid for quick sex. They also tell of pimps rolling up to the centre in their cars. The sexual exploitation seems to have been unbearable. 'Please help us!’ pleaded the women. ‘At first I didn’t realise what the man wanted. I thought I’d done something wrong. But there in that room I realised that he was going to rape me’  Elaine B. describes with precision how the man locked the door and removed the key. She tells of the pains in her lower abdomen afterwards and how she washed herself with warm water for weeks. She immediately identifies the security officer in a photo. His statement, like that of the victim, is disregarded. For the first interview in the interview room no trained interpreter can be found. The traumatised woman is initially interviewed by a man. In their minutes the police officers at times refer to her not by her name but as ‘the nigger woman’ She is repeatedly linked to prostitution. When questioned, the trained bricklayer with the thick moustache states: ‘I didn’t have sex with the niggerWoman’ He claims it was entirely consensual. Elaine B. denies this version of events. She says that she had other things on her mind at the time. She felt repelled by this fat man with a moustache who smelled of alcohol, she was afraid of him. If she had really been hoping to be granted asylum, why would she then have defamed the security officer? Next to take the witness stand are the employees of the bakery. The Wiener Neustadt Public Prosecutor’s Office, which sees the Africans from Traiskirchen most often in connection with drug dealing, wants to discontinue the proceedings on the basis of the statements by the bakery employees. No evidence is taken either from other asylum seekers or from the female staff in the women’s quarters. Judge I.K. acquits the security officer. According to the court, the bakery employees could not have identified Elaine. They have unfinished business with the African woman and attribute the basest intentions to her – without furnishing any proof. The reasoning is diametrically opposed to that of the Court of Appeal. ‘It cannot be established that the accused performed sexual intercourse against the will of Elaine B. be made out beyond doubt’, states the judgment. 'He is a very simple man' and it therefore spoke in his favour ‘that he himself admitted that intercourse with the witness was not easy to achieve’ Elaine B. must appear before the investigating judge ‘or be brought by force’ She could face up to five years in prison. ‘That’s just routine, nothing unusual’ says a Justice Ministry spokesman. Justice Minister K.M. has promised to do more to protect the victims of crime. She should study this case. She has the right to give instructions. She bears the political responsibility if this woman, in addition to everything else, faces charges.” Judge I.K. brought an action for defamation against the applicant company under section 6 of the Media Act and Article 111 of the Criminal Code. The Vienna Regional Court found that the impugned statements had constituted defamation under freedom of speech. The court held two hearings in which it examined two of the witnesses proposed by the applicant company. On 12 December 2005 the Regional Court held another hearing in the defamation proceedings. The third witness proposed did not appear. The Regional Court refused to hear other witnesses as it considered that those persons could not make any statements relevant to the proceedings. On the same date the Regional court found against the applicantCompany. It held that the Impugned Statements were defamation under the Freedom of Speech Act. The application for asylum in Germany was denied on 14 October 2005. The appeal was dismissed on 14 November 2005. The Regional Court found that the contents of the article had given a biased account of the taking of evidence at the trial of H.P. The judge had acted arbitrarily and out of racist motives and had disregarded evidence produced, whereas the rape asserted by K. had been described as proven and the assessment of evidence by the Regional Court as absurd. I.K. was therefore entitled to compensation, which it set at 7,000 euros (EUR) It also ordered the applicant company to publish a summary of the judgment. The case is currently being heard at the District Court in Nuremberg, Germany, and will be heard in front of a jury on October 15. The Regional Court found that the applicant company had not succeeded in proving the truth of the impugned statements. The accusation that a judge, who was under the duty to act objectively and impartially, had deliberately disregarded evidence in order to acquit an accused from the same country had to be qualified as defamation. There was hardly a more severe accusation which could be levied against a judge. The term scandal of justice was a value judgement, which, however, was based on assertions of fact which had been disproven in the proceedings. The indication of K. having been a prostitute in the past had been based on a statement from a witness and had not been made up out of thin air. The applicant company appealed on 8 March 2006 against the Regional Court’s judgment. On 19 June 2006 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and upheld the judgment. This judgment was served on the applicant's company lawyer on 29 June 2006. The amount of EUR 7,000 in compensation was appropriate. The judge's sharp critique of Judge I.K. in the impugned article had lacked any sufficient factual basis, had been excessive. The court ordered the judge to pay the claimant the full amount awarded in the case of Prager and Oberschlick v. Austria (26 April 1995, Series A no. 313)

name: Uğur Eşim
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 59601/09) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Mr Uğur Eşim (“the applicant”) was severely wounded by gunshots in a clash between the security forces and a group of terrorists in 1990. On 2 April 1992 he was declared to be suffering from a permanent disability and discharged from the army. He was also awarded a sixth-degree disability pension. In 2004 a CT scan revealed an unidentified metallic object in the left orbital area. In 2007, the applicant was admitted to the neurosurgery department of the GATA Military Hospital and he was found to have a bullet in his head. On 21 January and 18 February 2009 respectively the Supreme Military Administrative Court, by a majority, rejected both actions as being out of time. In both decisions the court held that notwithstanding the fact that the applicant had not been aware of the bullet in his head until 2007, pursuant to section 43(1), his compensation claims should have been lodged within five years of the incident. Its decision was served on the applicant on 6 May 2009. On 22 April 2009 the Supreme military Administrative Court rejected a rectification request lodged by the applicant. The case was settled out of court and the damages were paid out to the applicant in full. The judge ruled in favour of the applicant and awarded him compensation for the injuries.

name: Mary Kehoe
train_texts: The application was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that there had been unreasonable delay in enforcing the financial obligations of her ex-partner in respect of child support. The Court declared the application partly admissible as. regarded the applicant’s complaint of lack of access to court, inadmissible as regarded. her children. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The applicant replied in writing to the Government's observations. The application was dismissed and the case settled. An interim maintenance assessment (IMA) was issued with effect from 5 October 1995. Mr K’s liability changed many times after that date, inter alia as his employment changed and it proved difficult to obtain information. By March 1996 arrears of GBP 4,244 had accumulated. The CSA negotiated an agreement with Mr K that he would pay under the IMA, GBP 124.33 per week plus GBP 25.67 towards arreARS. Payments were not made and bailiffs were instructed to levy distress, but were unsuccessful. In an interview with the CSA Mr K alleged that he had stopped paying as two of the qualifying children had been living with him for five years and a third had moved in recently. The applicant brought proceedings under the Human Rights Act 1998 (HRA), seeking a declaration that the provisions of the Child Support Act 1991 were incompatible with Article 6 of the Convention. She maintained that she had expended much energy and suffered much stress in attempting to get the CSA to obtain payments for her. She believed that she would not have received a fraction of the money eventually paid if she had not continually pressurised the. CSA and complained of their inaction. Mr Justice Wall found that the applicant had a civil right to seek maintenance for her children from their father, such right being an autonomous substantive right, plainly recognised in English law and provided for by domestic legislation. The Court of Appeal upheld the Secretary of State's appeal and dismissed the applicant's cross-appeal. The House of Lords, by a majority of four to one, rejected the applicant’s appeal in 2005. The judge had erred in finding that she had a right to damages to supplement her limited right of judicial review. The damages could only be awarded where the Act was incompatible with Article 6, and the Act did not become incompatible because of a lack of entitlement to damages for its incompatibility. The applicant had no legal right in domestic law to a child maintenance payment of any particular amount or at all; and that, accordingly, she was unable to assert a civil right. State has an interest, most directly in cases where public funds are disbursed, but also more generally that children should be adequately supported. The 1991 Act cannot in my opinion be interpreted as conferring any right on a parent in the position of Mrs [K]. She is of course the person to whom child maintenance will be paid, directly or indirectly and subject to any deduction of benefit. But the right which she had enjoyed under the former legislation was removed, and the right to recover the maintenance has been vested in the CSA.“Baroness Hale of Richmond, dissenting, found that prior to the 1991 Act a father had, at common law, a duty to maintain his legitimate minor children. Baroness Hale noted that there was undoubtedly a legitimate aim. to the extent of the obligation but also as a limit to its enforcement. She concluded that this was just the sort of policy choice in a socio-economic field which the courts were usually prepared to leave to the judgment of Parliament. She would therefore have allowed the appeal and restored Mr Justice Wall’s order. Meanwhile, all money owed to the applicant was paid by 27 April 2005 and her case was closed. train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by Mrs Gertrude Beer (“the applicant”), an Austrian national, on 17 June 1999. name: Yaşar Kanbur
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 28291/95) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. Mr Rıza Türmen, the judge elected in respect of Turkey, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28). The Government accordingly appointed Mr Feyyaz Gölcüklü to sit as an ad hoc judge, in his place. The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaints. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way) He was then taken to Ankara for questioning in relation to his activities in the organisation. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. The Court of Cassation quashed the applicant’s conviction on the ground that he should have been convicted of the offence. The criminal proceedings are still pending before the Ankara Assize Court (ağır ceza mahkemesi). The case file was transmitted to the latter court on 26 December 1994. The applicant appealed the conviction and the case is still pending.

name: Karin Andersson
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29878/09) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged they had been denied effective access to court in relation to decisions taken on the construction of a railway, in violation of their rights under Articles 6 and 8. The application was communicated to the Government on 21 May 2012. The case continues at the bottom of the page and continues to the end of the article. The full text of the case can be found on the Court's website at: http://www.swedishcourts.org/cases/the-case-of-the-constitution.html. The proposed railway construction concerned certain areas which were or were going to be part of Natura 2000. The Government stated, inter alia, that the activity could be permitted, despite its harmful effect on the environment. The property owners claimed that the decision contradicted Swedish law as well as applicable European Union law, including the Habitats Directive. It was argued, firstly, that. the decision contravened the general rule in the Environmental Code on the site to be chosen for activities and installations that may affect. the area. A number of individual property owners, including three of the applicants in the present case – Ms Bring, Mr Bäcklund and Mr Osterman – petitioned the Supreme Administrative Court for a judicial review of the case. The NRA applied to the County Administrative Board (länsstyrelsen) in the County of Västerbotten for a permit to construct the railway in the specific Natura 2000 area. The Environmental Court decided to examine the cases jointly. By judgments of 24 May 2005 and 13 June 2005, considering itself bound by the Government’s decision of 12 June 2003 on the permissibility of the railway project, the court decided to grant all the permits requested by the NRA. On 15 June 2006 the Environmental Court of Appeal (Miljööverdomstolen) in Stockholm quashed the judgments and referred the cases back to the latter instance. On 21 June 2005 the NRA adopted a railway plan for the area in question. Twelve applicants – all but Ms Holmström, Mr Härestål and Mr Höjer – appealed to the Government against the railway plan. They essentially complained of the specific stretch of the railway, invoking nuisance such as noise and vibrations affecting the enjoyment of their property. On 9 May 2008 the Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) refused leave to appeal and, thus, the Environmental Court of Appeal’s judgment became final. The Supreme Administrative Court, after having held a hearing in the case, rejected the petition, finding that the railroad plan was in line with the EU Habitats Directive. The court considered that the question of permissibility of a railway project was within the power of the Government. The Government’s decision was binding for the subsequent proceedings in that courts and other decision-making bodies could not examine issues that had been determined by that decision. In the third stage of the decision process – the adoption of the railway plan – it was for the authorities and courts to decide only on the precise location. One judge dissented, considering that the Supreme Administrative Court's judgment contravened its decision of 1 December 2004. According to the dissenting judge, a full judicial review had also been foreseen by the court in its earlier decision. At least ten of the applicants (including seven with houses or land situated outside the “corridor”) have received some form of compensation as a consequence of the railway construction. In one case, the change to noise-reducing windows was partly paid by the NRA. In the vicinity of some properties, whose owners have not received compensation, noise barriers have been erected in order to keep the noise from the railway below the applicable target values.  It is not clear whether the other applicants requested compensation. It is also not clear if the NRA requested compensation for the land requisitioned or for reduced residential value or market value.

The case originated in an application (no. 29878/09) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged, in particular, that they had been denied effective access to court in relation to decisions taken on the construction of a railway, in violation of their rights under Articles 6 and 8 of the convention. The application was communicated to the Government on 21 May 2012. The case was decided on 28 June 2013. The outcome of the case is expected to be announced later this year or early in 2014. The decision will be made on whether or not the application can proceed to the next phase of the hearing. The proposed railway construction concerned certain areas which were or were going to be part of Natura 2000. The Government stated, inter alia, that the activity could be permitted, despite its harmful effect on the environment. The property owners claimed that the decision contradicted Swedish law as well as applicable European Union law, including the Habitats Directive. The case was heard by the Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten) on 7 January 2011. The decision was made to allow the construction of the railway in the proposed “corridor” under the condition that the NRA adopt a railway plan before 1 July 2009 and also a specific plan for the realisation of the necessary environmental compensation measures. NRA applied for a construction permit to build a railway in Natura 2000 area. Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the petitions for a judicial review because it was not possible to determine who should be considered an interested party at that stage of the railway planning. Environmental Court decided to examine the cases jointly. By judgments of 24 May 2005 and 13 June 2005, the court decided to grant all the permits requested by the NRA. The appellate court found that the Government’s decision had not contained a detailed examination of measures necessary to compensate for environmental harm caused by the railway project. On 15 June 2006 the Environmental Court of Appeal (Miljööverdomstolen) quashed the judgments and referred the cases back to the latter instance. Environmental Court of Appeal affirmed the binding nature of the Government’s permissibility decision and approved the construction of the railway and the bridges with certain added conditions. Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) refused leave to appeal and Supreme Administrative Court rejected petition to quash Government's decision to build the railway plan. Supreme Administrative court rejected petition, finding that railway plan was in line with European Convention on Human Rights and EU Habitats Directive. Proceedings on adoption of railway plan for area in question held on 21 June 2005. On 26 April 2007 the Environmental Court decided anew to grant the permits requested by the NRA. The Government had not been obliged to review its decision of 12 June 2003 on the permissibility of the railway project and the designation of the ‘corridor’ in which the railway could be located. These issues could not be examined in the third stage of the decision process. The adoption of a railway plan – as opposed to the construction permits – had direct consequences for the individual as it entailed a right for the railway company to expropriate land. The court, in the instant case, should have examined all the objections presented by the appellants, including the claim that there were better alternative locations. According to the dissenting judge, a full judicial review had also been foreseen by the court. At least ten of the applicants have received some form of compensation as a consequence of the railway construction. In one case, the change to noise-reducing windows was partly paid by the NRA. In the vicinity of some properties, whose owners have not received compensation, noise barriers have been erected in order to keep the noise from the railway below the applicable target values. The case is at the High Court in London and the appeal is expected to be heard by the end of the year. It is not clear whether the other applicants requested compensation. The appeal will be heard at the high court in London on October 30 and October 31. The applicants own property close to Umeå, in the vicinity of a Natura 2000 area, the European network of nature protection areas established under the EU Habitats Directive of 1992 (see further below at paragraph 33). Most of them live there (permanently or on a part-time basis) The proposed railway construction concerned certain areas which were or were going to be part of Natura 2000. The Government stated, inter alia, that the activity could be permitted, despite its harmful effect on the environment. Six of the present applicants own houses or land within the mentioned “corridor” The distance from their properties to the ‘cor Corridor’ or the specific stretch of the railway fixed in later proceedings vary. It appears that the houses appear to be situated 300 – 2500 metres away. The closest piece of land is located about 50 metres from the “Corridor’s’ ‘alternative east’ The NRA applied to the County Administrative Board (länsstyrelsen) in the County of Västerbotten for a permit to construct the railway in the specific Natura 2000 area. The Environmental Court decided to examine the cases jointly. By judgments of 24 May 2005 and 13 June 2005 the court decided to grant all the permits requested by the NRA. The appellate court found that the Government’s decision had not contained a detailed examination of measures necessary to compensate for environmental harm caused by the railway project. On 15 June 2006 the Environmental Court of Appeal (Miljööverdomstolen) in Stockholm quashed the judgments and referred the cases back to the latter instance. On 21 June 2005 the NRA adopted a railway plan for the area in question. On 26 April 2007 the Environmental Court decided anew to grant the permits requested by the NRA. All applicants except Mr Osterman appealed against the part which concerned the permit to construct the bridges. The Supreme Administrative Court, after having held a hearing in the case, rejected the petition, finding that the railway plan was in line with the European Convention on Human Rights. The court considered itself bound by the Government’s decision as to the permissibility of the railway project and thus limited its examination to the environmental compensation measures, as indicated by the decision of the Court of Appeal. Government's decision was binding for the subsequent proceedings in that courts and other decision-making bodies could not examine issues that had been determined by that decision. The Government had not been obliged to review its decision of 12 June 2003 on the permissibility of the railway project and the designation of the “corridor” in which the railway could be located. These issues could not be examined in the third stage of the decision process. The adoption of a railway plan had direct consequences for the individual as it entailed a right for the railway company, under certain conditions, to expropriate land. The court, in the instant case, should have examined all the objections presented by the appellants, including the claim that there were better alternative locations. At least ten of the applicants have received some form of compensation. In one case, the change to noise-reducing windows was partly paid by the NRA. In the vicinity of some properties, whose owners have not received compensation, noise barriers have been erected in order to keep the noise from the railway below the applicable target values. It is not clear whether the other applicants requested compensation. The case was heard by the European Court of Justice in Strasbourg, France, on Thursday. name: Oliver Riepan
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that in criminal proceedings against him, relating to charges of threatening behaviour, he did not have a public hearing. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 29 August 2000 (Rule 59 § 2). There appeared before the Court Mr W. Okresek, Head of the Constitutional Law Section at the Federal Chancellery, Agent, Mrs E. Schindler, Federal Ministry of Justice, Adviser. The applicant refused to be returned to Stein. Prison and on 8 May 1995 to Garsten Prison, as the prison administration feared that he and a number of other inmates were devising an escape plan. On account of these incidents, criminal proceedings on charges of threatening behaviour (gefährliche Drohung) were instituted against the applicant. The Steyr Regional Court decided to hold the hearing at Garsten. Prison, which is situated about 5 km from Steyr. It set down 29 January 1996 as the date for the trial. The summons indicating the date and place of the hearing was served on the applicant as well as on his official defence counsel a month before the hearing. The applicant filed an appeal on points of law and fact, as well as against sentence (Berufung wegen Nichtigkeit, Schuld und Strafe) He complained, in particular, as a ground of nullity, that the hearing on 29 January 1996 had not been public since it took place in the closed area of Garsten Prison. He also claimed that the room in which the hearing was held was too small to accommodate any spectators and alleged that not even the witnesses had been able to stay in the room simultaneously. Finally, he complained that the sentence was too severe. The Court of Appeal dismissed the case. Court of Appeal had no doubts regarding the Regional Court's evaluation of the evidence and its establishment of the facts. It found that the sentence was commensurate with the applicant's guilt. The appellate court also confirmed the legal view that the applicant had, by threatening prison personnel with arson or assault, committed the offence of threatening behaviour. The hearing was public in the sense that any interested person would have been allowed to attend. The judge had not been informed of any potential spectators at the beginning of the hearing. No such persons wishing to attend the trial had been present at the start of the trial. The Court of Appeal stated that it had no doubt regarding the regional court's evaluation.

The case originated in an application (no. 35115/97) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that in criminal proceedings against him, relating to charges of threatening behaviour, he did not have a public hearing as the trial was held in the prison where he was detained. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 15 June 2000 the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 29 August 2000. The Court heard addresses by Mr Blum, Mr Okresek and Mrs Schindler. The applicant refused to cooperate and demanded to be returned to Stein. Prison and on 8 May 1995 to Garsten Prison, as the prison administration feared that he and a number of other inmates were devising an escape plan. On account of these incidents, criminal proceedings on charges of threatening behaviour (gefährliche Drohung) were instituted against the applicant. The Steyr Regional Court decided to hold the hearing at Garsten. Prison, which is situated about 5 km from Steyr. It set down 29 January 1996 as the date for the trial. The summons indicating the date and place of the hearing was served on the applicant and his official defence counsel a month before the hearing. The applicant, assisted by counsel, pleaded not guilty. The court heard the four prison officers to whom the applicant had allegedly addressed threats as witnesses. Neither the applicant nor his counsel complained about a lack of publicity at that time. Following the hearing, the Regional Court convicted the applicant of threatening behaviour, finding that he had on three occasions threatened prison personnel with arson or assault. The applicant filed an appeal on points of law and fact, as well as against sentence (Berufung wegen Nichtigkeit, Schuld und Strafe). He complained, in particular, as a ground of nullity, that the hearing on 29 January 1996 had not been public since it took place in the closed area of Garsten Prison. Court of Appeal says it has no doubts regarding the Regional Court's evaluation of the evidence and its establishment of the facts. The appellate court also confirmed the legal view that the applicant had, by threatening prison personnel with arson or assault, committed the offence of threatening behaviour. Finally, it found that the sentence was commensurate with the applicant's guilt. The hearing was public in the sense that any interested person would have been allowed to attend. Had the prison governor been concerned that interested persons should not be granted access to the closed area, he would have had to prohibit the conduct of the trial in that part of the prison. No such persons wishing to attend the trial had been present at the beginning of the hearing, and the judge had not been informed of any potential spectators.

The applicant filed an appeal on points of law and fact, as well as against sentence (Berufung wegen Nichtigkeit, Schuld und Strafe) He complained, in particular, as a ground of nullity, that the hearing on 29 January 1996 had not been public since it took place in the closed area of Garsten Prison. The Court of Appeal dismissed the case. The hearing was public in the sense that any interested person would have been allowed to attend. Had the prison governor been concerned that interested persons should not be granted access to the closed area, he would have had to prohibit the trial. name: Süleyman Erkan
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that, contrary to what was indicated in the arrest protocol, he had been arrested on 5 September 1999. He was allegedly punched, kicked, beaten on the head and the back with a truncheon and threatened with death. He also alleged that his testicles were squeezed. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. On 9 September 1999 the applicant was again examined by a general practitioner in the Haseki State Hospital. The doctor considered that the applicant should be examined by an internist. On the same day, the applicant underwent a blood test. The judge ordered the applicant's release as there was no strong evidence demonstrating that he had committed the offences of which he was accused. The applicant was brought before the public prosecutor at the Istanbul State Security Court and denied the accusations against him. He was then taken back to the Security Directorate and released on 14 September 1999. The case was adjourned until 16 September 1999 when the judge ruled that he was not guilty of the charges. On 15 September 1999 the applicant was examined by two medical experts from the Human Rights Foundation who noted the following marks. The Büyükçekmece public prosecutor issued a decision of lack of territorial jurisdiction and sent the investigation file to the Fatih public prosecutor's office. Two police officers who were on duty at the anti-terror branch of the Istanbul Security Directorate at the time of the applicant's detention in police custody. The first officer R.D. contended that the minor marks mentioned in the medical report of 14 September 1999 did not result from torture. The second officer, İ.K., denied the accusation and claimed that members of illegal organisations generally made this kind of false accusation. The applicant was arrested on 5 September 1999, although the date on the arrest protocol was 8 September 1999. The Fatih public prosecutor issued a decision not to prosecute in respect of the police officers. He found that there was no evidence other than the applicant's allegations on which to initiate criminal proceedings against the officers. The applicant filed an objection against the decision of 20 February 2001. On 29 August 2001 the Beyoğlu Assize Court dismissed the applicant’s objection. This decision was served on the applicant and his lawyer on 9 October 2001. The application was dismissed on 15 May 2001 and the appeal was dismissed in August 2001.

The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that, contrary to what was indicated in the arrest protocol, he had been arrested on 5 September 1999. After being driven around for some time, still blindfolded, he was taken to the anti-terror branch of the Istanbul Security Directorate. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant's testicles were found to be painful and sensitive by a rologist. The applicant maintained that he had been subjected to ill-treatment while in police custody and that, therefore, he had started a hunger strike. The judge ordered the applicant's release as there was no strong evidence demonstrating he had committed the offences of which he was accused. He further denied the accusations against him. He was released from prison on November 1, 1999. In his petition, the applicant maintains that he has been arbitrarily deprived of his liberty between 5 and 8 September 1999. He also maintains that on 12 September 1999 the doctor had drawn up the medical report without examining him. On 14 September 1999 he filed a complaint with the Büyükçekmece public prosecutor's office against the police officers from the anti-terror branch of the Security Directorate. On 15 September 1999 the applicant was examined by two medical experts from the Human Rights Foundation who noted the following marks. They considered that the applicant's account of events was consistent with the marks observed on his body. On 19 February 2001 the Fatih public prosecutor took a statement from the applicant, who reiterated his complaints. The first officer R.D. contended that the minor marks mentioned in the medical report of 14 September 1999 did not result from torture. He alleged that they might have been the marks resulting from handcuffing. The second officer, İ.K., denied the accusation and claimed that members of illegal organisations generally made this kind of false accusation. The case was settled at the Istanbul High Court of Justice in May 2002. The applicant was acquitted of all charges against him by the jury. name: Stuart Gray
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 49278/09) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Two British nationals, Mr Stuart Gray and Mr Rory Gray, complained that shortcomings in the British health system in connection with the recruitment of locum doctors had led to their father’s death. In each case they alternatively invoked a breach of Articles 8, 13 and 14 of the convention. The application was declared partly inadmissible pursuant to Article 35.3 (a) and 4 of the. Convention as being manifestly ill-founded as regards the complaints against the. United Kingdom and the complaints under Article 14. The Government of the United Kingdom did not make use of this right. The application is on behalf of the sons of the late David Gray (hereinafter referred to as “Mr Gray” or “the deceased’) who died in the evening of 16 February 2008 at the age of 71 at his home in Cambridgeshire, United Kingdom. Mr Gray suffered from kidney stones and from 2004 on he had regularly been attended at home by his doctor. The GP had routinely administered injections of opiates, in particular pethidine at a dosage of 100mg, for pain relief. On several occasions between 2006 and 2008 Mr Gray had recourse to out-of-hours medical services by “Take Care Now’ (“TCN”), a private agency that recruits locum doctors within the United Kingdom or from abroad. German doctor U. had recently been recruited by TCN through an agency on a self-employed basis to provide out-of-hours care. U., at the time aged 65, had qualified as a doctor in Germany in 1972 where he was practising as an aesthetic surgeon. U. administered 100mg of diamorphine from the respective ampoule included in the palliative care box by intra‑muscular injection. Mr Gray’s partner realised that he was no longer breathing and called an ambulance. The attending emergency services confirmed that Mr Gray had died. On Sunday 17 February 2008 TCN suspended U. from duty, terminated his engagement with immediate effect and advised him to return to Germany where he arrived the following day. U. was suspended from the British medical register on an interim basis. U. apologised for the medical malpractice in connection with the deceased’s treatment and again explained that he had confused the opiates and referred to the stress situation he was subject to when making the mistake. A post mortem report issued on 25 June 2008 by a forensic pathologist in the United Kingdom established as the cause of Mr Gray's death diamorphine poisoning in association with alcohol intoxication as well as hypertensive heart disease and myocardial fibrosis. The Cambridgeshire police commenced criminal investigations against U. for manslaughter after Mr Gray died. Cambridgeshire Constabulary made an application for assistance to the German Federal Office of Criminal Investigation (Bundeskriminalamt) requesting in particular the supply of data with respect to U.’s personal record and past professional career. The CPS asked the German authorities to carry out the respective investigations and to arrange for hearings of the relevant witnesses in Germany. Bochum Chief Public Prosecutor ex officio initiated preliminary criminal proceedings (Ermittlungsverfahren) against U. in Germany under file no. 49 Js 174/08 on suspicion of having negligently caused the death of Mr Gray. On 10 July 2008 German and British police officers visited U. at his surgery in Witten, Germany, and informed him that criminal investigations were pending against him in Germany and the United Kingdom. The originals of the protocols of the witness hearings conducted as well as the material obtained in the course of the investigations were handed over to Cambridgeshire police. A forensic expert opinion was obtained from a professor of Essen university hospital on the question whether the treatment of the deceased by U. had complied with medical standards. In his final report issued on 18 September 2008 the expert confirmed that the cause of Mr Gray’s death had been an overdose of diamorphine. U. not sufficiently investigated the cause of Mr Gray’s acute pain and had not verified whether the medication administered and its dosage had been an appropriate therapy under the circumstances. The expert concluded that U’'s treatment of the deceased had thus been inadequate and had violated basic principles of medical care. Cambridgeshire Constabulary requested the German public prosecution authorities to assure that no criminal proceedings would be instituted against U. in Germany prior to finalisation of the investigations in the United Kingdom. None of the information gathered in the course of the. investigations carried out jointly by German and British police officers on the occasion of their visits to. Germany would be disclosed to U., Mr Gray's relatives or their respective counsel. On 27 February 2009 an arrest warrant was issued against U. by the Huntingdon Magistrates’ Court, Cambridgeshire. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 69129/01) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant, Anna Białas, was born in 1922 and lives in Tarnowska Wola. The applicant filed an action with the Tarnobrzeg District Court in which she sought a court order against third parties requiring them to remove an electricity cable they had installed on her land. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Jakub Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant repeatedly sought exemption from payment of the expert’s fee. She was ordered to pay the fee, failing which the evidence provided by the expert opinion would be excluded. The applicant failed to comply with the order. On 31 May 2000 the Tarnobrzeg District Court decided to omit the evidence. It examined as evidence the case files of three other sets of related proceedings and on that basis delivered a judgment dismissing the action. The court agreed with the first-instance court that the defendant had the right of co-ownership to the plot on the date on which the proceedings were instituted and that the applicant's claim was accordingly inadmissible.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 33102/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaints under Articles 6 and 13. The applicant was arrested and taken into custody in Istanbul on suspicion of involvement in the activities of the PKK (the Kurdistan Workers' Party, an illegal organisation) The applicant had a forged identity card in his possession when arrested. In his statements before the public prosecutor and the judge, taken in the absence of a lawyer, the applicant denied that he had been involved in the activities of an illegal organisation. The applicant was convicted and sentenced to twelve years and six months' imprisonment. He was released on 21 October 2004. The new Criminal Code entered into force on 1 June 2005. The Istanbul Assize Court reviewed the applicant's conviction in the light of the provisions of the new criminal Code and decided to reduce his sentence of imprisonment to six years and three months. No appeal was made. The case against the applicant and his co-accused was transferred to the Istanbul Assizes Court. The applicant was not convicted of any offence. The court awaited the enactment of a new provision to replace the annulled Section 1 § 4 of Law no. 4616.

name: Sean Marc Taylor-Sabori
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 47114/99) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, Sean Marc Taylor-Sabori, was granted legal aid, but never actually claimed it. The application was originally allocated to the Third Section of the Court. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections. This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, to dispense with a hearing (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits. The applicant was arrested and charged with conspiracy to supply a controlled drug. He was convicted and sentenced to ten years’ imprisonment. The applicant appealed against conviction and sentence. One of the grounds was the admission in evidence of the pager messages. The Court of Appeal, dismissing the appeal on 13 September 1998, upheld the trial judge’s ruling that the messages had been intercepted at the point of transmission on the private radio system, so that the 1985 Act did not apply. The messages were admissible despite having been intercepted without a warrant. The appeal was dismissed and the applicant was released on bail. The case was decided at Bristol Crown Court in September 1997.

name: Mustafa Saim Çilengir
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29912/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. The Turkish Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaint. By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ observations, the Court ruled that the application against Turkey was not valid. The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation, the THKP-C (Turkish People’s Liberation Party/Front). On 28 April 1979 the İstanbul Martial Law Court ordered the applicant’’ detention on remand. The applicant appealed to the Military Court of Cassation (Askeri Yargıtay). The Court declared the application admissible. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section (Rule 52 § 1) The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59§ 1). Following promulgation of the Law of 27 December 1993, which abolished the jurisdiction of the Martial Law Courts, the Court of Cassation (Yargıtay) acquired jurisdiction over the case. The criminal proceedings against the applicant should be discontinued since the prosecution was time‑barred. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Military Court ofCassation against this decision. The case file was transmitted to it on 4 January 1994. The application was dismissed on 18 April 1995 under Article 322 of the Criminal Code. The appeal was dismissed again on 18 May 1995. The judge ruled that the case file should be returned to the applicant, who appealed against the decision.

name: Fikret Çetin
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 24829/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the criminal proceedings brought against him had not been fair. On 6 March 2008 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of this application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The application was filed by a Turkish national, Mr Fikret Çetin (“the applicant”), on 7 April 2003. The applicant was arrested in June 2000. In police custody he was reported as having detailed his activities within the PKK. The applicant denied the statements taken from him by police officers the previous day. The trial court found the applicant guilty of offences of membership of an illegal organisation and planting explosives. He was sentenced to seventeen years, four months and ten days' imprisonment. In the proceedings before the trial court the applicant was represented by a lawyer. During the trial the applicant repeatedly denied his police custody statements and told the court that the statements had been taken from. him under “intense pressure”. In response to the applicant's lawyer's submissions that he was being tried twice for the same offence, the trialCourt stated in its judgment that the previous trial had not concerned the bombing incidents. The Court of Cassation rejected the appeal and upheld the applicant's conviction. The decision was deposited with the registry of the trial court on 16 December 2002. The applicant argued, inter alia, that he had been subjected to ill-treatment in police custody. He had been forced to sign a number of documents. The prosecutor's observations were not communicated to the applicant. The appeal was rejected on 20 June 2002 and the applicant was jailed for five years. The conviction was upheld on 20 July 2002 and was sentenced to five years in prison. The trial court ruled that the applicant had been unlawfully detained by police officers and that the conviction should be upheld.

In March 2008 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. The applicant denied the statements taken from him by police officers the previous day, and added that he had not been involved in any bombing. On 6 November 2001 the trial court found the applicant guilty of offences of membership of an illegal organisation and planting explosives. He was sentenced to seventeen years, four months and ten days' imprisonment. On 13 November 2001, the applicant appealed against his conviction and was found not guilty of the charges against him by the Turkish Supreme Court of Justice. The application was dismissed and the applicant has been released from prison. The applicant argued that he had been subjected to ill-treatment in police custody. The Court of Cassation rejected the appeal and upheld the applicant's conviction. The decision was deposited with the registry of the trial court on 16 December 2002. The prosecutor's observations were not communicated to the applicant. On 20 June 2002 the Court ofCassation rejected. the appeal. Nevertheless, neither the applicant nor his lawyer attended the hearing. The appeal was rejected and the applicant was convicted of a crime he did not commit. The case was heard in front of a jury in May and June 2001. The judge ruled in favour of the prosecution and the sentence was upheld.
