name: Steven Phillips
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 41087/98) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, inter alia, that the statutory assumption made against him by the court which issued a confiscation order violated his right to the presumption of innocence. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. It was declared partly admissible on 30 November 2000. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 8 February 2001 (Rule 59 § 2). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Ms H. Fieldsend, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr D. Perry, Counsel, Ms M. Dyson, Home Office, Mr P. Vallance, Advisers. An inquiry was conducted into the applicant’s means, pursuant to section 2 of the Drug Trafficking Act 1994 (“the 1994 Act’ – see below) On 12 July 1996 he was sentenced to nine years’ imprisonment in respect of this offence. The investigation officer concluded that the applicant had benefited from drug trafficking and that the total benefit was GBP 117,838.27. The applicant was found to have become a director of a newsagents business in July 1992 of which his parents were the sole shareholders. He was the registered owner of five cars, of an estimated total value of approximately GBP 15,000, and spent GBP 2,000 on a BMW 520i in October 1995. The applicant filed a written statement in response, in which he denied having benefited from drug trafficking. He explained that in 1990-91 he had been convicted of car theft and required to pay GBP 25,000 to the insurance company which had indemnified the victims. He claimed that he had sold the house for GBP 50,000. to X in order to clear this debt and had used the GBP 12,000 residue from the sale to purchase the newsagents premises for his parents because he owed them money too. When he was released from prison in April 1994 he began trading in telephones; this was the source of theGBP 17,000 in his building society account. He denied owning any of the cars registered in his name. Judge found the prosecution’s allegation that the applicant still owned the house to be correct. Judge held that the purported purchase payment of GBP 50,000 had in fact been a benefit of drug trafficking. Instead of calling as witnesses the alleged purchaser of the house, X, the applicant had called only himself, his father and a solicitor. There are real indications on the civil basis of proof that [X] was complicit in the crime of which the accused was convicted. A mobile phone at the heart of the arrangements for the haulage of the drugs was registered in the name of [X]. Just as the jury did not believe Mr Phillips, neither do I. What has happened here is a device of just the sort providing a cover to explain the transfer of money. The judge said it was impossible to see any sensible reason why the applicant did not cash a cheque. The judge assessed the applicant to have benefited from drug trafficking to the extent of GBP 91,400. ‘I am satisfied that the GBP 11,400 must be treated as a benefit,’ the judge said. “For the reasons that I have given above I am satisfied [the applicant] is in fact the applicant,” the judge added. The jury returned a verdict of guilty of two counts of fraud, one of perverting the course of justice and the other of misconduct in a public office. The judge allowed him three years in which to pay the confiscation order, with a period of two years’ imprisonment to be served in default of payment. His application to renew leave to appeal against conviction and sentence was refused on 22 January 1998 after a full hearing before the Court of Appeal. The judge is satisfied that the GBP 50,000 which he said in evidence was what such a property was worth in 1992, that is to say during the long, flat period. Since I am satisfied as to GBP 100,000 realisable sums, that figure exceeds theGBP 91,400 and under section 5 I find the amount to be recovered to be that figure.

The applicant alleged, inter alia, that the statutory assumption made against him by the court which issued a confiscation order following his conviction for a drug offence violated his right to the presumption of innocence. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court and was declared partly admissible on 30 November 2000. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 8 February 2001. The Court heard addresses by Mr Pearse Wheatley and Mr Perry. An inquiry was conducted into the applicant’s means, pursuant to section 2 of the Drug Trafficking Act 1994 (“the 1994 Act’ – see below) On 12 July 1996 he was sentenced to nine years’ imprisonment in respect of this offence. The investigation officer concluded that the applicant had benefited from drug trafficking and that the total benefit was GBP 117,838.27. The applicant was found to have become a director of a newsagents business in July 1992 of which his parents were the sole shareholders. He was the registered owner of five cars, of an estimated total value of approximately GBP 15,000, and spent GBP 2,000 on a BMW 520i. The applicant denies having benefited from drug trafficking. He sold the house for GBP 50,000 to X in order to clear this debt. He used the GBP 12,000 residue from the sale to purchase the newsagents premises for his parents because he owed them money too. When he was released from prison in April 1994 he began trading in telephones. He denied owning any of the cars registered in his name, claiming variously that each had been purchased and sold on behalf of a friend or stolen without insurance. The applicant filed documentary evidence and affidavits in support of his claim no longer to own the house. He held that the purported purchase payment of GBP 50,000 had in fact been a benefit of drug trafficking. The judge commented generally that, in seeking to displace the assumption, the applicant had failed to take obvious, ordinary and simple steps which would clearly have been taken if his account of the facts had been true. Just as the jury did not believe Mr Phillips, neither do I, the judge said. It is a device of just the sort providing a cover to explain the transfer of money which one would expect to find in concealing benefit from drug trafficking, he added. The judge says he cannot see any reason why the applicant did not cash a cheque. He also finds the purchase of a share of a business for GBP 50,000 entirely without documentation simply unbelievable. The judge assessed the applicant to have benefited from drug trafficking to the extent of GBP 91,400. He next calculated the value of the realisable property held by the applicant as follows: “For the reasons that I have given above I am satisfied that [the applicant] is in fact the applicant’s property.” The judge also said that he did not believe that the accused had any interest in the remaining shop premises. In the absence of a current valuation, but taking judicial notice of a recent modest recovery in the housing market after a long, flat period, I am satisfied that the GBP 50,000 which he said in evidence was what such a property was worth in 1992. In view of the difficulties inherent in realising the applicant’s share of the family business, the judge allowed him three years in which to pay the confiscation order, with a period of two years’ imprisonment to be served in default of payment. name: Snjezana Vostic
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38549/97) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the court decisions in compensation proceedings for detention on remand violated the presumption of innocence. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 19 June 2001 the Court declared the application admissible. This case was assigned to the newly composed First Section. The case was decided in favour of the applicant. Upon the pronouncement of the acquittal, the applicant was released. She requested compensation for her detention on remand. The Wels Regional Court, with the same composition as above, dismissed the applicant’s claim. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Linz Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) She argued that section 2 (1)(b) of the 1969 Act was incompatible with Article 6 § 2 of the Convention. On 20 June 1997, the court dismissed her appeal. The decision was served on the applicant after her acquittal had become final on 17 December 1996. It considered that only a decision which expressed the view that the accused was guilty could violate the presumption of innocence. ‘Nor does the principle of the presumption. of innocence prevent the prosecuting authorities from suspecting someone of having committed an offence’ “The trial court thus rightly held that the testimony given by the parents of the appellant, whose alibi related to the night of 31 March to 1 April 1996, was not credible.” “Snjezana Vostic’s own testimony to the effect that she had last seen Sejdo Nadarevic in mid-February 1996 was in the end disproved by the witnesses who gave evidence at the trial”“It was still possible that Snjezanna Vostic's gun had been the murder weapon; furthermore, inconsistencies remain unresolved.’ “In the instant case it was precisely such a suspicion concerning Vostic that had not been wholly dispelled...”

name: Türkan Yavuz
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 67137/01) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits. The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 52 § 1) The Court will decide on both the admissibility and merits of the application. The application was filed by a Turkish national, Ms Türkan Yavuz (“the applicant”), on 8 February 2001. It is alleged that the applicant and her husband were arrested and taken into custody on suspicion of their membership of an illegal organisation. On 21 May 1997 the applicant was brought before the public prosecutor at the İstanbul State Security Court. She acknowledged the contents of her police deposition. She stated that during her custody, four or five police officers had sexually harassed her by touching her breasts and buttocks. She claimed that she was also punched. She affirmed that she would be able to recognise them if she were to meet them again. The applicant was released and no criminal proceedings were brought against her. An investigation was instigated into the alleged ill-treatment and the criminal proceedings against police officers. The court considered that it lacked competence to examine the allegations of ill‑treatment brought by the applicant and Mr E.Y. The applicant was arrested in July 1997 and charged with ill-treatment. She claimed she was attacked by police officers who pulled her hair and hit her, particularly between her shoulders. She maintained that they stripped her naked in front of her husband and that she was molested and sexually harassed. The officers refuted the accusations against them, claiming that both the applicant and Mr E.Y. had resisted arrest and that, as a result, they could have sustained some injuries. The applicant’s request, to intervene as a third party, on 13 February 1998 was accepted by the court. In the hearing held on 13 October 1998 the applicant's representative informed the court that they waived their right to have the applicant”s witness Mr ŞT. heard. The court decided not to hear him. The applicant’s husband testified in favour of the applicant. He submitted that they were all subjected to systematic torture whilst in police custody. He claimed that their clothes were ripped, their feet were squeezed, they were hosed with pressurised water and that their heads were pushed into a pool of water. had taken place during her arrest. The court concluded that, apart from the findings in the medical reports, there were no other signs of injury and that those mentioned in these reports could have been sustained during the arrest of the complainants. On 4 October 2000 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the Assize Court.

The case originated in an application (no. 67137/01) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The applicant was arrested and taken into custody on suspicion of their membership of an illegal organisation, namely the TKP/ML0. According to the search protocol drafted on the same day by the police officers and signed by the applicant, the police found a number of documents, guns, ammunition and dynamite. The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section of the Court. The applicant was brought before the public prosecutor at the İstanbul State Security Court on 21 May 1997. She acknowledged the contents of her police deposition. However, she stated that during her custody, four or five police officers had sexually harassed her by touching her breasts and buttocks. She claimed that she was also punched. She affirmed that she would be able to recognise them if she were to meet them again. The applicant was released and no criminal proceedings were brought against her. The court considered that it lacked competence to examine the allegations of ill‑treatment brought by the applicant and Mr E.Y., and transferred the investigation file to the Fatih public prosecutor’s office. The applicant claimed that she was attacked by police officers who pulled her hair and hit her, particularly between her shoulders. She maintained that they stripped her naked in front of her husband. She claimed that, during her interrogation, one of the police officers threatened her with rape, while all the officers insulted her verbally and also threatened to accuse her of murder if she refused to co-operate. The applicant stated that it was impossible for her to provide witnesses since she was in custody, incommunicado, away from all eyewitnesses. Mr E.Y.’s testimony was taken by the Fatih public prosecutor on 27 October 1997. Between 25 November 1997 and 1 June 1999, the court held eight hearings. The applicant’s husband testified in favour of the applicant. He submitted that they were all subjected to systematic torture whilst in police custody. The court concluded that, apart from the findings in the medical reports, there were no other signs of injury and that those mentioned in these reports could have been sustained during the arrest of the complainants. On 4 October 2000 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the Assize Court. The judge said that the evidence before it did not suffice to convict the accused police officers. The applicant was acquitted of all charges against her on 1 June 1999. She was sentenced to ten years in prison.

name: Collette Hemsworth
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 58559/09) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants mainly complained under Article 2 that there had been an unlawful use of lethal force against the deceased, Mr John Hemsworth, and that the State had not fulfilled its procedural investigative obligations in that respect. The application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. On 11 January 2012 the Irish Government declined to exercise their right to intervene (Article 36 § 1 of. the Convention and Rule 44 § 1). John Hemsworth died on 1 January 1998 after suffering severe headaches and tingling in one arm. The RUC began an investigation supervised by the Independent Commission for Police Complaints (“ICPC”) The Attorney General ordered the Coroner to hold an inquest. A pre-inquest hearing was held in June 2001 to hear submissions on the implications of the judgments of this Court of 4 May 2001 in certain cases concerning deaths in Northern Ireland (Hugh Jordan v. the United Kingdom, no. 24746/94, (extracts) and McKerr v. McKerr). The applicants claimed that the original pathologist later expressed his agreement with these later two expert opinions. The first applicant applied for legal aid for the inquest under the Lord Chancellor’s Extra-Statutory Scheme. On 5 June 2001 she began a judicial review action. The action continued in order to challenge that limitation on funding. On 7 January 2003 the High Court found against her as did the Court of Appeal (9 March 2005) On 26 April 2004 the High court found in her favour. The first applicant was legally represented, as she was for all domestic proceedings. The hearing was adjourned given the possibility of the referral of those cases to the Grand Chamber of this Court. The applicants claimed that, during that hearing, the Coroner advised that there was no evidence that the deceased had been struck by RUC officers. The first applicant applied to the Coroner to recuse himself. The Coroner refused but indicated that he would receive further representations as to why RUC witnesses were required. On 9 March 2009 the High Court found in her favour: a new Coroner was to be appointed. The inquest began on 21 September 2009. It did not sit each day and certain witnesses were unavailable through ill-health. On 8 October 2009 the jury discharged the jury due to evidence which had emerged. It emerged that Officer M had been a member of the RUC at the time of the alleged assault. He was also the Deputy Investigation Officer and, in addition, he was due to be called as a witness. The first applicant therefore requested and received Officer M’s journal entries on the police investigation. Private G told the Coroner that he had seen an officer in the RUC Blues OSU assaulting a civilian with a baton in an area close to the location of Mr Hemsworth’s alleged assault. Private G had also told Officer M that a senior military officer, as well as a senior RUC officer, had told him that he should not report this incident to his superiors. The Coroner ordered the PSNI to prepare a paginated and indexed bundle of all material held by them in relation to the death of John Hemsworth, including any documentation held in connection with Private G. The inquest was scheduled to begin on 21 January 2010. The first applicant obtained an expert medical report which found that marks on the deceased's face and back were consistent with the allegations of assault by police baton. The inquest into the death of John Hemsworth began on 16 May 2011. In May 2011 a supplementary expert report was submitted. On 27 May 2011 the inquest jury rendered its verdict. It found the medical causes of death to be cerebral infarction and thrombosis of the right internal carotid artery. The Coroner announced that he would refer the matter to the Director of Public Prosecutions (“DPP”) and ensured the production, from public funds, of a transcript of the inquest proceedings. On 3 February 2012 the DPP’s office acknowledged the referral. Further to the applicants’ queries, on 23 April 2012 the Coroner confirmed the referral and on 14 May 2012 the case was adjourned. The Government submitted that the matter was the subject of ‘active consideration’ by the DPP. The Police Ombudsman reviewed the police file. In his report of 1 May 2007 he considered that the medical experts did not agree on the extension of a causal link between the July 1997 injuries and the subsequent death. There was no evidence that any RUC officer was responsible for John Hemsworth’s death and he could identify nothing further that he could do to take the matter forward. On 5 September 2001 the applicant initiated civil proceedings against the PSNI and on 10 August 2011 a Notice of Intention to Proceed was served.

He was also the Deputy Investigation Officer and, in addition, he was due to be called as a witness. The Coroner obtained and disclosed Officer M’s journal entries on the police investigation. He had interviewed a soldier (Private G) in 2000. Private G had told Officer M that, on the day of the assault, he had been drinking. The Coroner was advised by the Crown Solicitor’s Office that all documentation in relation to Private G was destroyed in August 2009. The Coroner ordered the PSNI to prepare a paginated and indexed bundle of all material held by them. Officers unconnected with the original investigation should conduct this disclosure exercise. The inquest was scheduled to begin on 21 January 2010. On the second and third days of the inquest, two jurors advised the Coroner of connections to the police. The first applicant obtained an expert medical report which found that marks on the deceased's face and back (apparent from photographs taken after the alleged assault) were consistent with the allegations of assault. John Hemsworth died on 7 July 1997. Inquest jury accepted that his injuries included fractures to both the right and left hand sides of his jaw bone, tramline bruising to the left jaw, neck and lower left side of his back. Coroner referred the matter to the Director of Public Prosecutions (“DPP”) on 3 February 2012. On 23 April 2012 the Coroner confirmed the referral and the case was referred to the DPP pursuant to section 35(3) of the Criminal Justice (Northern Ireland) Act 2002. The DPP’s office acknowledged the referral on 3 January 2012. The Government submitted that the matter was the subject of ‘active consideration’ by the DPP. The Police Ombudsman reviewed the police file. In his report of 1 May 2007 he considered that the medical experts did not agree on the extension of a causal link between the July 1997 injuries and the subsequent death. There was no evidence that any RUC officer was responsible for John Hemsworth’s death and he could identify nothing further that he could do to take the matter forward. On 5 September 2001 the applicant initiated civil proceedings against the PSNI and on 10 August 2011 a Notice of Intention to Proceed was served.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 49867/08) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Uzbek national. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr A. Yılmaz, a lawyer practising in Istanbul. The Turkish Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent. On 7 April 2015 the Chamber decided, under Rule 54 § 2 (c) of the Rules of Court, to invite the parties to submit further written observations on the admissibility and merits of the application. The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Turkey. He fled from Uzbekistan to Tajikistan because of pressure from the police. In 2005 he arrived in Iran, where he settled in Zahedan. In 2007 he fled from Iran following deportation threats. He entered Turkey illegally through Van and went to Ankara to apply for refugee status. He was given a temporary residence permit until 24 September 2008 and was ordered to report to the police three times a week for signature. He claimed that the threats had been a response to certain disagreements with the Iranian authorities over their living conditions. It appears that the other Uzbek asylum seekers who had fled. The applicant was allegedly ill‑treated and threatened by the police during deportation. Iran together with the applicant were granted similar certificates and permits after following the same procedural steps. The asylum seekers contacted some other Uzbeks who had managed to escape deportation from Turkey and obtained the ransom fee. The smugglers made them walk for three days to Yüksekova, a town close to the Iranian border of Turkey, where they were released. They requested legal advice from the Van Bar Association, which, along with two Turkish non-governmental organisations, published a report on 28 September 2008 regarding the Uzbek asylum seekers’ collective expulsion. It was argued in the report, inter alia, that the expulsion of the Uzbek by the Turkish State authorities had had no legal basis. The applicant has been living in Turkey in hiding and his application for refugee status under the mandate of the UNHCR is still under consideration. He has not received any information from the Turkish authorities as to his request for asylum. The applicant has not been able to apply for asylum or to obtain a temporary residence permit due to a lack of information. The UNHCR also informed the applicant’s representative that the applicant, along with a number of other Uzbek nationals, had been illegally deported to Iran and that the asylum claim was under review. The application for asylum in Turkey has been denied by the Turkish government. The asylum claim has been declined by the UNHCR. The applicant applied for asylum in Turkey in December 2007. His application was registered and he was asked not to leave the city of Van. He was subsequently deported to Iran, a safe third country, where he was recognised as a refugee by the UNHCR. According to a document signed by two police officers and one military officer, submitted by the Government, twenty-nine Uzbek and Afghan nationals, including the applicant, were deported on 12 September 2008. He cannot appoint a lawyer to undertake the necessary legal and procedural actions on his behalf before the domestic authorities as he does not possess the necessary identity documents required to issue a power of attorney before a notary public.

The applicant went to the police station for signature, as part of his weekly routine, on 12 September 2008. He was allegedly ill‑treated and threatened by the police during deportation. After crossing the border to Iran on foot, the Uzbek asylum seekers, including the applicant, were captured and held hostage by people smugglers. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 49867/08) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’) on 17 October 2008. The applicant’s representative requested that the Court adopt an interim measure, under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, to stop his threatened deportation to Iran or Uzbekistan. The Government were further requested to submit copies of administrative courts’ decisions in cases concerning removal of asylum seekers rendered subsequent to the entry into force of the Foreigners and International Protection Act (Law no. 6458) On 16 July 2015 the Government replied to the submissions of the applicant. The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Turkey. He fled from Uzbekistan to Tajikistan in 1999 because of pressure from the police. In 2005 he arrived in Iran, where he settled in Zahedan. In 2007 he fled from Iran following deportation threats. He claimed that the threats had been a response to certain disagreements with the Iranian authorities over their living conditions. On 18 November 2007 the applicant entered Turkey illegally through Van and went to Ankara to apply for refugee status at the UNHCR. The Van office issued him with an asylum seeker certificate. Subsequently, he registered with the Van police headquarters and started the domestic temporary asylum procedure. Thereafter he was given a temporary residence permit until 24 September 2008. The applicant went to the police station for signature, as part of his weekly routine, on 12 September 2008. He and other Uzbeks were forcibly deported to Iran. Iran together with the applicant were granted similar certificates and permits after following the same procedural steps. The applicant was allegedly ill‑treated and threatened by the police during deportation. The asylum seekers, including the applicant, were captured and held hostage by people smugglers, who demanded 5,000 U.S. dollars to spare their lives and to release them. They managed to escape by contacting others who had escaped and paid the ransom fee. They walked for three days to Yüksekova, a town close to the Iranian border of Turkey, where they were released. The applicant has been living in Turkey in hiding since 2008. He has not received any information from the Turkish authorities as to his request for asylum. His application for refugee status under the mandate of the UNHCR is still under consideration. The applicant’s representative sent letters to the Human Rights Commission of the Parliament of Turkey, the Deputy Governor of Van and the Ministry of the Interior. The UNHCR informed the applicant that the applicant and other Uzbek nationals had been deported to Iran in compliance with the legislation in force. On 4 December 2013 and 28 March 2014 he was interviewed by officers from the UNHCR’S Ankara office regarding his application for Refugee Status. The applicant applied for asylum in Turkey in December 2007. He was subsequently deported to Iran, a safe third country, where he was recognised as a refugee by the UNHCR. He does not possess the necessary identity documents required to issue a power of attorney before a notary public. He cannot appoint a lawyer to undertake the necessary legal and procedural actions on his behalf before the domestic authorities as he does not have the necessary documents to do so. The Government says the applicant was not deprived of his liberty and that his identity documents were not confiscated. The applicant does not want to be deported again to Iran like the other Uzbek asylum seekers who were deported in October 2008.
